facts.note: Table 2, p.5. Closing CFR rises £47.131m in 2026/27 (£67.861m capital spend via borrowing less £20.730m MRP), then plateaus.
Table 2, p.5. Closing CFR less PFI and IFRS 16 lease liabilities (which fall from £134.766m to £109.801m over the plan).

Table 3, p.6. Net new borrowing of £120.988m planned in 2026/27 alone — the paper is essentially flat in the current year (net £-3.962m) then externalises hard in the first year of the plan. No PWLB/LA/LOBO split published in the strategy.
Table 3, p.6. Balance-sheet identity ties to the pound across all four years: CFR − external borrowing − PFI/lease liabilities = internal borrowing.

Para 3.1.8, p.12. Rochdale itself frames call risk as arising 'if / when market rates are above the current level being paid on those loans (average of 4.55%)'. Their advisor's 20-year PWLB certainty rate forecast (Table 5, p.10) is 4.75%-4.85% for every quarter of the plan — the trigger they describe is already satisfied on their advisor's own numbers. No call disclosed in this paper; no call-date detail given. £69m sits among the largest LOBO stocks in the library (Newcastle £141m is the biggest; Rochdale's £69m is second-tier).

facts.value: Arling Close (p.10): Bank Rate 3.50% Mar-26 → 3.25% Jun-26 held to Sep-28; 5y PWLB 3.80-3.85%; 10y PWLB 4.25-4.35%; 20y PWLB 4.75-4.85%; 50y PWLB 4.45-4.50%
facts.note: Table 5, p.10. Rates quoted net of HM Treasury's 0.2% Certainty Rate discount (paper says 'The PWLB rates quoted above are net of HM Treasury's Certainty Rate which enables the authority to benefit from a 0.2% reduction to the standard rate'). Advisor commentary: 'long-term gilt yields to remain broadly at current levels on average'. Essentially a rate-stability call across the plan.

facts.value: Net Interest Budget £12.009m (2025/26) → £13.633m → £14.108m → £14.296m; a 1% rate rise adds £2.797m to £3.584m across the plan
facts.note: Table 6, p.13. A 1% rise is a 23-25% uplift on the net interest budget across the plan. Against the £6.951m 'Interest Cost with Internal Borrowing' line, the uplift is 40% in 2025/26 — the marginal rate on new external borrowing does most of the work.
Table 9, p.23. Not split GF/HRA in this paper. Rises 0.54 points over the plan on the back of the internal-borrowing unwind.
Table 4, p.7. Both limits include IFRS 16 lease elements — paper flags these as estimates pending full impact assessment.

facts.value: Asset Life Method (continuing); pre-1 April 2008 CFR at 2% straight line (50-year write-out); 20 years for Ministerial Direction / non-asset expenditure; annuity for Invest to Save case-by-case
facts.note: Section 3.5, pp.24-27. VRP over-provision £0.137m at 31 March 2026. Compliant with April 2024 MRP guidance revisions; post-7 May 2024 capital loans MRP no lower than recognised expected credit loss.
Table 10, p.24. Only the >10-year bucket has a lower floor (25%). Under-12-month cap of 70% would accommodate substantial temporary borrowing.

facts.value: MMF (AAA) £20m normal / £30m special; but capped at £15m per MMF going into 2026/27 (advisor advice); Local incl GM/GMCA/Police & Fire £15m/£20m; DMO unlimited; >365-day limit £75m; third-party loans upper limit £130m

items: Budget Report and Medium Term Financial Strategy — Appendix 9 Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 (includes MRP)

summary.text:
An under-borrowed council planning to externalise £121.0m of internal borrowing in a single year. Underlying borrowing requirement grows from £487.486m to £550.631m over the plan; external borrowing rises from £251.158m to £396.336m; internal borrowing shrinks from £236.328m to £154.295m. The 2026/27 step is £120.988m of net new borrowing — the current year is essentially flat. Balance-sheet identity ties to the pound across all four years (CFR − external borrowing − PFI/lease liabilities = internal borrowing).

The distinctive item is a £69m LOBO block at 4.55% average (paragraph 3.1.8, p.12). Rochdale itself frames the call trigger as market rates above 4.55%; their advisor's own 20-year PWLB certainty rate forecast (Table 5) is 4.75%-4.85% across every quarter of the plan, 20-30bp above the trigger. No call disclosed in this paper. Across the councils we have read this year the library holds twelve LOBO calls, every one refused and repaid — Oldham 6.70% and 7.67%, Wolverhampton 6.19% / 6.21% / 6.26%, plus Kent, Tameside, Newport, Bridgend, Harrow, Staffordshire, Reading and Newcastle. Rochdale's £69m sits among the larger LOBO stocks in the library (Newcastle £141m is the biggest).

No loan-level annex is published, so we cannot tie our PWLB file (36 loans, £130.070m at 3.5991% at 31 March 2026) to a Rochdale-published PWLB total. The paper's £251.158m closing borrowing includes the £69m LOBO block plus PWLB plus LA temp; the split is not disclosed. Loan-book reconciliation therefore does not go in the email.

status.note: The paper prints only a general contact block (council@rochdale.gov.uk, 01706 647474). Strategy Owner Samantha Smith (Director of Corporate Services) and Strategy Author Neil Helliwell (Senior Accountant, Tax & Treasury) are named on p.1; neither address is published in the paper. Officer email needed before send. Anchor on next Corporate Overview & Scrutiny or Cabinet treasury item (quarterly monitoring; next date not published in this paper).

officer.subject: Your £69m LOBO block, and the twelve calls we've logged elsewhere
officer.body:
Dear Samantha,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are some thoughts ahead of your next quarterly treasury item at Corporate Overview & Scrutiny or Cabinet. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your strategy is one of the clearer ones we've read this year — the question-headed structure ("What limits does the Council have on borrowing?", "How much will the Council need to borrow?") makes it much easier for a non-treasury reader to follow, and this note is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

Leading with the LOBO block because your own paragraph 3.1.8 sets the frame. You hold £69m of historical LOBOs at a 4.55% average, and you say plainly that the call trigger arrives once market rates sit above that. On Arling Close's own Table 5 they already do: the 20-year PWLB certainty rate is forecast at 4.75% through to 4.85% for every quarter of the plan, 20 to 30 basis points above the LOBO average. On the twelve LOBO calls we've logged across the councils we've read this year, every one has been refused and repaid — Oldham was offered 6.70% and 7.67%, Wolverhampton 6.19%, 6.21% and 6.26%, and Reading had its Dexia LOBO called at 6.26% in January and repaid within the week. None of that is a recommendation — the visible pattern is officers doing the arithmetic and repaying — but the £69m puts you in the top tier of LOBO stocks we hold (Newcastle at £141m is the largest), and it is the sort of backdrop you can only see across the sector, not from any one paper.

The borrowing plan itself is the other thing that stood out. Current-year net borrowing is essentially flat at minus £4m; Table 3 then externalises £121m net in 2026/27, £17m in 2027/28 and £7m in 2028/29 — the internal borrowing position drops from £236m to £170m in one year and to £154m by 2028/29. That is a large single-year externalisation, and it rides on Arling Close's view that the 10-year PWLB certainty rate barely moves (4.35% in March, 4.30% in June, 4.25% by September and held there). Bank Rate today is 3.75% — unchanged since your strategy went to Council on 25 February — and the 1-year OIS is around 4.10%, pricing a rise rather than a further cut. Nothing about that has to change today, but it is the sort of test a member on Corporate Overview & Scrutiny could reasonably put: which forecast are you now working to for the £121m.

A smaller thing that may be useful. Your Table 6 shows a 1% rate rise adding £3.220m to the 2026/27 net interest budget on a £13.633m base — a 24% uplift on that line. Against the £9.148m "Interest Cost with Internal Borrowing" figure the sensitivity is 35%. We publish the monthly local-authority borrowing detail at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity, which shows what other councils have actually been paying for short and medium PWLB paper since your strategy went to Council — worth a look before the £121m starts to flow.

One fair disclosure on our side. Your paper does not publish a loan-level annex, so we cannot tie our own PWLB file to a Rochdale-published PWLB total. Nothing to raise on your side — flagging it so you know what the platform can and can't verify from the strategy alone.

None of it needs a meeting or a subscription, and the rates page at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard takes ten seconds to check. On training, four look most relevant to Rochdale: LOBO loans, for the £69m block and the call-risk framing you set out; Interest rate risk, for the Table 6 sensitivity; Strategic PWLB borrowing, for the £121m 2026/27 externalisation; and our liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data — worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
